title: Fatigue in a 34-year-old woman with type 1 diabetes: an underactive thyroid and a macrocytic anaemia
desc: This station involves a focused fatigue history and a thyroid-focused examination of a 34-year-old gardener and part-time paramedic student with type 1 diabetes. The candidate then interprets her full blood count, thyroid function tests and antibodies, inflammatory markers and electrolytes. They explain autoimmune hypothyroidism, start levothyroxine safely, plan the work-up of her macrocytic anaemia and safety-net in general practice.
focus: Fatigue history in general practice: recognising autoimmune (Hashimoto) primary hypothyroidism with a macrocytic anaemia in a woman with type 1 diabetes, and starting thyroxine safely
stem: You are a GP registrar in a general practice in a regional town. Jenny Berry, a 34-year-old gardener and part-time paramedic student, has booked an appointment because she has been feeling tired.
tasks: Take a focused history from Jenny and perform a focused examination, telling the examiner what you are examining and why (10 minutes).

The examiner will give you Jenny's full blood count, thyroid function tests and thyroid antibodies, inflammatory markers and electrolytes. Interpret them, then outline your management approach and safety netting (5 minutes).
patient:
Role: You are Jenny Berry, 34, a gardener and part-time paramedic student. You are tired and a little flat, but polite and cooperative. You think you are probably just doing too much. Do not volunteer details: give each answer only when asked. You agree to be examined. The examiner gives the examination findings below when the candidate says what they would examine.

Opening line: "I just feel really weak and lacking in energy. It's been going on for a few months now."

The tiredness (give only when asked):

  • Onset and course: it came on gradually about 3 months ago and is getting worse.
  • What it feels like: "I just feel really weak and lacking in energy." Your legs feel heavy. It is not sleepiness, and you do not nod off during the day or at the wheel.
  • Severity: if asked to score it, 4 out of 10.
  • What changes it: nothing makes it better or worse, not even a weekend's rest.
  • Cause: if asked what you think is causing it: "I'm not sure."
  • Impact: "It's just making it hard for me to work and study." You feel a bit foggy when you study.

Other symptoms you have noticed (give each only when asked about it):

  • You have put on about 4 kg in 3 months without eating more.
  • You feel the cold more than everyone else and wear a jumper when others don't.
  • You are constipated: you open your bowels every 3 or 4 days, which is not normal for you.
  • Your skin is dry, and more hair than usual comes out in the shower and on your brush.
  • Periods: irregular over the last few months, coming every 5 to 7 weeks. The flow is normal, not heavy. Your last period started 3 weeks ago. You are not in a relationship and have not been sexually active since your partner died, so you could not be pregnant. You use no contraception.
  • Mood: you feel a bit flat and down lately. You still enjoy time with your daughter and your garden when you have the energy. No thoughts of harming yourself or ending your life. You sleep 8 hours but wake unrefreshed. Your appetite is unchanged.

Things you do not have (if asked):

  • No heat intolerance, palpitations, tremor, sweating or diarrhoea.
  • No lump or pain in the neck, no trouble swallowing, and no change in your voice. No sore throat or viral illness recently.
  • No change in your sugars and no hypos. No dizziness on standing, salt craving, nausea, vomiting, tummy pain or darkening of the skin.
  • No black stools or bleeding from the bowel. No bloating or diarrhoea.
  • No weight loss, night sweats, fevers, cough, lumps or bumps. No known contact with TB, and no overseas travel.
  • No chest pain, breathlessness beyond the tiredness, or ankle swelling. No snoring that you know of (you sleep alone), and no waking up gasping.
  • No joint pain, rash, mouth ulcers or urinary symptoms.
  • No numbness, pins and needles or unsteadiness. No tingling in your hands.

Past medical history:

  • Type 1 diabetes since you were 17. It is well managed: your last HbA1c, 3 months ago, was "about 7". Your eye and foot checks are up to date.
  • Childhood asthma. You now use a salbutamol (Ventolin) inhaler only before exercise (you call it "my Ventolin").
  • If asked: no previous thyroid problems, neck surgery or radiation to the neck. Your only pregnancy was your daughter, 8 years ago.

Medicines: insulin glargine 20 units at night and insulin aspart with meals (you count carbohydrates); salbutamol (Ventolin) inhaler before exercise. No other medicines, vitamins or supplements. Never taken amiodarone or lithium.

Allergies: penicillin (rash as a child) and cats (sneezing, itchy eyes). Vaccinations: up to date (needed for your paramedic placements).

Family history: your mother has type 1 diabetes. Your father and your sister both had asthma as children; your sister's was severe. Your brother is healthy. Your daughter, aged 8, is healthy. No thyroid problems that you know of.

Social history:

  • You live with your 8-year-old daughter in a regional town. Your partner died 5 years ago; you have grieved and are coping.
  • You work as a gardener and study paramedicine part time.
  • You were a social smoker in your 20s and do not smoke now.
  • Alcohol: 2 glasses of wine every night "to unwind". If asked to quantify: normal-sized glasses, about 3 standard drinks a night, so about 20 a week.
  • Exercise is now limited by the tiredness. Takeaway twice a week; otherwise you cook, and you eat meat (not vegetarian).
  • Support: "somewhat connected". A couple of good friends in town, and your sister lives an hour away.

Ideas, concerns, expectations:

  • Idea: not sure; maybe you are just doing too much with work, study and parenting on your own.
  • Concern: keeping up with your work and course, and being there for your daughter.
  • Expectation: to find out what is going on, probably with some blood tests.

Question to raise in Part 1: "Do you think it's just because I'm doing too much?"

Exam findings (examiner: give only when the candidate says what they examine):

  • General: looks tired but alert, a little slow to respond. Mild puffiness around the eyes. Normal voice. Affect slightly flat but reactive.
  • Observations: HR 56/min, regular. BP 128/86 mmHg sitting, 126/84 mmHg standing (no postural drop). RR 14/min. SpO2 98% on room air. Temperature 36.1 °C. Weight 72 kg (notes show 68 kg three months ago), height 165 cm, BMI 26.4 kg/m². Capillary glucose 7.2 mmol/L.
  • Hands: cool and dry. No tremor. Palmar creases not pigmented. Tinel and Phalen tests negative.
  • Face, skin and hair: dry, coarse skin on the arms and shins. Diffuse thinning of the scalp hair and of the outer eyebrows. Pale conjunctivae. No jaundice. Buccal mucosa not pigmented; tongue normal.
  • Neck: a small diffuse goitre, visible with the neck extended. It moves up on swallowing, not on tongue protrusion. It is firm, rubbery, smooth and non-tender, with no discrete nodule. The lower border is palpable, the trachea is central, and Pemberton's sign is negative. No cervical lymphadenopathy. No bruit.
  • Cardiovascular and respiratory: heart sounds dual with no murmur or rub. JVP not raised. No peripheral oedema. Chest clear.
  • Abdomen: soft and non-tender. No organomegaly or masses.
  • Neurological: power 5/5 throughout; she rises from a chair without using her arms. Ankle jerks present with a slow relaxation phase on both sides. Knee reflexes normal. Vibration and joint position sense normal at both great toes. Romberg negative.

check.x: Professionalism
Hand hygiene, introduction and role, confirms Jenny's identity, explains the purpose of the consultation and confidentiality, and gains consent for the examination.
Empathic and non-judgemental: acknowledges the strain of working, studying and parenting alone, responds sensitively to her partner's death, and asks about alcohol without judgement.
History
Characterises the fatigue:

kids.x: Onset and course: gradual over 3 months and getting worse.
Character: weakness and lack of energy rather than sleepiness (no daytime sleep attacks).
Severity and modifying factors: 4/10, nothing makes it better or worse.
Impact: making it hard to work and study.

check.x: Asks about symptoms of hypothyroidism:
check.d: Award when at least two of the three kids are covered.

kids.x: Weight gain (about 4 kg) and cold intolerance.
Constipation, dry skin and hair loss.
Menstrual change: irregular periods, last period, and whether pregnancy is possible (not sexually active).

check.x: Screens for depression: low mood, anhedonia, sleep, and thoughts of self-harm or suicide [feels flat, still enjoys her daughter and garden, wakes unrefreshed, no suicidal thoughts].
Asks screening questions for other causes of fatigue:
check.d: Award when at least four of the five kids are covered.

kids.x: Hyperthyroidism and the thyroid: heat intolerance, palpitations, tremor, neck lump or pain [none].
Anaemia: diet, menstrual loss, black stools or rectal bleeding [takeaway twice a week, eats meat, normal flow, no GI bleeding].
Diabetes control and adrenal insufficiency: change in sugars or hypos, dizziness on standing, salt craving, nausea, skin darkening [none].
Malignancy, infection and TB: weight loss, night sweats, fevers, cough, lumps, TB contact [none].
Cardiorespiratory causes and sleep apnoea: chest pain, breathlessness, ankle swelling, snoring or witnessed apnoeas, daytime sleepiness [none].

check.x: Takes the past medical history: type 1 diabetes since 17, well managed (asks about hypos and the last HbA1c), childhood asthma; previous thyroid disease, neck surgery or radiation, recent pregnancy [none].

Takes the medication history: insulin glargine and aspart, salbutamol (Ventolin) inhaler before exercise, no drugs affecting the thyroid (amiodarone, lithium) or supplements; allergy to penicillin (rash).
check.d: Credit, but do not require: cat allergy; vaccinations up to date.

check.x: Takes the family history, asking specifically about thyroid and autoimmune disease [mother type 1 diabetes; no known thyroid disease].
check.d: Credit, but do not require: father and sister childhood asthma; brother and daughter healthy.

check.x: Takes a social history:
check.d: Award when at least three of the four kids are covered.

kids.x: Alcohol quantified in standard drinks: 2 glasses of wine every night, about 20 a week.
Smoking: social smoker in her 20s, none now.
Diet and exercise: takeaway twice a week, not vegetarian; exercise limited by fatigue.
Home, work and supports: lives with her 8-year-old daughter in a regional town, partner died 5 years ago, gardener and paramedic student, somewhat connected.

check.x: Explores ideas, concerns and expectations: unsure of the cause (perhaps doing too much), worried about work, study and caring for her daughter, expects blood tests; answers her question without false reassurance.
Examination
General inspection and vital signs with weight, BMI and a capillary glucose [HR 56 regular, BP 128/86, temperature 36.1 °C, weight 72 kg (up 4 kg), BMI 26.4, glucose 7.2].
check.d: Credit, but do not require: lying or sitting and standing BP to look for adrenal insufficiency [no postural drop].

check.x: Examines the hands, skin, face and hair: cool dry skin, conjunctival pallor, periorbital puffiness, thin scalp hair and outer eyebrows; looks for tremor and for pigmentation of the palmar creases or buccal mucosa [no tremor, no pigmentation].

Examines the thyroid: inspects from the front with a swallow and tongue protrusion, palpates from behind for size, consistency, tenderness and nodules, checks the cervical nodes and trachea, and auscultates for a bruit [small diffuse, firm, rubbery, non-tender goitre; no nodule, nodes or bruit].
check.d: Credit, but do not require: Pemberton's sign or percussion for retrosternal extension [negative].

check.x: Tests the reflexes, looking for delayed relaxation, and proximal power [slow-relaxing ankle jerks; power 5/5, rises from a chair].
check.d: Credit, but do not require: Tinel and Phalen tests for carpal tunnel syndrome [negative]; vibration and joint position sense [normal].

check.x: Brief cardiorespiratory examination with a check for peripheral oedema [normal heart sounds, clear chest, no oedema].
Interpretation

Full blood count: macrocytic anaemia (Hb 104 g/L, MCV 118 fL) with normal white cells and platelets; states that an MCV this high is more than hypothyroidism usually causes, so B12 or folate deficiency (pernicious anaemia with her autoimmunity) and alcohol must be considered.
Thyroid function: TSH 52 mIU/L (high) with free T4 4.3 pmol/L (low) is overt primary hypothyroidism.
check.d: Credit, but do not require: free T3 at the lower limit.

check.x: Antibodies: positive anti-TPO and anti-thyroglobulin confirm autoimmune (Hashimoto) thyroiditis; TRAb negative.
ESR mildly raised, in keeping with the anaemia (and raised immunoglobulins in autoimmune disease); normal CRP is in keeping with Hashimoto thyroiditis and argues against subacute thyroiditis.
Electrolytes: normal sodium and potassium make adrenal insufficiency less likely but do not exclude it; normal renal function.
Gives the diagnosis as Hashimoto thyroiditis causing overt primary hypothyroidism, with a macrocytic anaemia needing work-up.

Names at least three differentials, each with a feature for or against from this case: B12 deficiency (pernicious anaemia), alcohol or folate deficiency, subacute thyroiditis, depression, Addison disease.
Management

Explains in plain language: the immune system has damaged the thyroid, this is more common with type 1 diabetes, it is very treatable with a daily tablet taken for life, and energy improves over weeks to months.
Starts levothyroxine:
check.d: Award when both kids are covered.

kids.x: Dose: young with no heart disease, so a full replacement dose of about 1.6 micrograms/kg (ideal body weight) daily, about 100 micrograms, taken for life.
kids.d: Accept a lower starting dose with titration.

kids.x: How to take it: on an empty stomach 30 to 60 minutes before breakfast, at least 4 hours apart from iron or calcium.
kids.d: Credit, but do not require: keep to the same brand.

check.x: Monitors: TSH 6 to 8 weeks after starting and after each dose change, titrating to a TSH in the reference range, then yearly once stable, avoiding over-replacement.
Works up the macrocytic anaemia with B12 and folate (with intrinsic factor antibodies), and does not give folate alone before B12 deficiency is excluded or treated.
check.d: Credit, but do not require: reticulocyte count, review of the pending blood film, iron studies, LFTs and GGT.

check.x: Screens for associated autoimmune disease: coeliac serology (tTG-IgA with total IgA); checks a morning cortisol before starting thyroxine if there is any suspicion of adrenal insufficiency.
Diabetes: advises more frequent glucose checks because insulin needs may change as the thyroid is treated.
check.d: Credit, but do not require: HbA1c may be unreliable while she is anaemic.

check.x: Alcohol: brief intervention, advising no more than 10 standard drinks a week and no more than 4 on any one day (NHMRC).
Pregnancy planning: tell the GP before trying to conceive or as soon as pregnant, because the levothyroxine dose needs to rise and TSH needs checking early.
check.d: Credit, but do not require: aim for a TSH below 2.5 mIU/L before conception.

check.x: Safety netting
Warns about too much thyroxine: palpitations, tremor, feeling hot, weight loss or poor sleep need a GP review; chest pain, a racing irregular heartbeat or collapse needs 000.
Gives other red flags in plain words:
check.d: Award for at least two of the four.

kids.x: Increasing drowsiness, confusion or feeling very cold and slowed: 000 or ED.
Breathlessness, numbness or pins and needles, unsteadiness or memory change (anaemia or B12 deficiency): GP within days.
A rapidly growing neck lump, trouble swallowing or breathing, or a hoarse voice: urgent review.
Worsening mood or thoughts of self-harm: Lifeline 13 11 14, the GP, or ED.

check.x: Arranges follow-up: review of the further blood tests in about a week and TSH in 6 to 8 weeks.
check.d: Credit, but do not require: written information.

part2.lead: Jenny had the blood tests you requested and has come back a week later to discuss them. Here are her results.
part2.patient:
Jenny is not part of Questions 1 to 3. She is back in the room for Question 4 and asks these while the candidate explains:

  • "Will I have to take tablets forever?"
  • "Is this because of my diabetes?"
  • "I'd like another baby one day. Does this change anything?"

Be relieved to hear it is treatable. If alcohol is raised, accept the advice: "I suppose two glasses every night has crept up."

handover.label: Full blood count
handover.result: Lab comment: macrocytic anaemia. Blood film to follow.
handover.model:
Read: Hb 104 g/L (low) with MCV 118 fL and MCH 40.8 pg (high), normal MCHC and a raised RDW (anisocytosis), which fits a megaloblastic process such as B12 or folate deficiency. White cells and platelets are normal. This is an isolated macrocytic anaemia.

For Jenny: hypothyroidism can cause a mild macrocytosis, but an MCV of 118 is more than it usually causes. B12 or folate deficiency is likely, and pernicious anaemia is more likely in someone with autoimmune thyroiditis and type 1 diabetes. About 20 standard drinks a week may contribute, and a takeaway diet may lower her folate. The anaemia adds to her fatigue and pallor. Her neurological examination is normal.

What it changes: check B12, folate, intrinsic factor antibodies, reticulocytes, review the pending blood film (hypersegmented neutrophils, oval macrocytes), iron studies, LFTs and GGT. Do not give folate alone until B12 deficiency is excluded or treated. If the macrocytosis persists without a cause once she is euthyroid, refer to haematology.

handover.label: Thyroid function tests and thyroid antibodies
handover.model:
Read: TSH 52 mIU/L (high) with free T4 4.3 pmol/L (low): overt primary hypothyroidism. Free T3 is at the lower limit, because conversion of T4 to T3 rises to compensate, so T3 falls late. Anti-TPO and anti-thyroglobulin antibodies are strongly positive, and TRAb is negative.

For Jenny: this is Hashimoto (autoimmune) thyroiditis. It explains her fatigue, weight gain, cold intolerance, constipation, dry skin, hair loss, irregular periods, low mood, bradycardia, slow-relaxing reflexes and diffuse firm goitre. A high TSH shows the pituitary is responding, so this is primary, not central, hypothyroidism.

What it changes: start lifelong levothyroxine and recheck TSH in 6 to 8 weeks. The goitre is diffuse with no nodule, so no ultrasound is needed. Autoimmunity clusters, so screen for coeliac disease and pernicious anaemia.

handover.label: Inflammatory markers and electrolytes
handover.model:
Read: ESR 34 mm/h, mildly raised; CRP 3 mg/L, normal. Sodium, potassium, urea and creatinine are normal.

For Jenny: The mildly raised ESR is explained by the anaemia; the CRP is normal, as expected in Hashimoto thyroiditis, and subacute thyroiditis is unlikely (non-tender gland, no thyrotoxic phase, normal CRP, strongly positive antibodies). Normal sodium and potassium argue against, but do not exclude, adrenal insufficiency, and she has no hyponatraemia from severe hypothyroidism.

What it changes: the inflammatory markers need no further work-up. The normal electrolytes and lack of adrenal features support starting thyroxine now. If in doubt, check a morning cortisol first.

ask: You are now handing over to your supervising GP. Please give an ISBAR handover of Jenny Berry, including your interpretation of these results.
What is your most likely diagnosis, and what else would you consider? Justify your answer.
Outline your management of Jenny now, here in general practice.
Jenny is back in the room. Before she goes home, explain her diagnosis to her, answer her questions, and tell her what to watch for and what follow-up you will arrange.
expect:
• Identify: self, GP registrar; Jenny Berry, 34.
  • Situation: 3 months of worsening fatigue. Results show overt primary hypothyroidism and a macrocytic anaemia.
  • Background: type 1 diabetes since 17, well controlled on basal-bolus insulin; childhood asthma; penicillin allergy; about 20 drinks a week. Weight gain, cold intolerance, constipation, dry skin, hair loss, irregular periods, low mood. HR 56, diffuse firm non-tender goitre, slow-relaxing reflexes.
  • Assessment: TSH 52 and fT4 4.3 mean overt primary hypothyroidism. Positive anti-TPO and anti-Tg mean Hashimoto. Hb 104 with MCV 118 is too macrocytic for thyroid alone, so B12/folate or alcohol. ESR mildly raised (anaemia), CRP normal. Na and K are normal.
  • Recommendation: start levothyroxine; B12, folate, IF antibodies, coeliac serology; TSH in 6 to 8 weeks.

Most likely: Hashimoto thyroiditis causing overt primary hypothyroidism, with a macrocytic anaemia. For: hypothyroid symptoms, HR 56, diffuse firm goitre, slow reflexes; TSH 52, fT4 4.3, positive antibodies; type 1 diabetes.

  • B12 deficiency (pernicious anaemia): MCV 118 is high for thyroid disease alone and she has two autoimmune diseases. Her neurology is normal and B12 is not yet measured.
  • Alcohol or folate deficiency: about 20 drinks a week and a takeaway diet.
  • Subacute thyroiditis: hypothyroidism with a goitre, but the gland is non-tender, she had no thyrotoxic phase, her CRP is normal and her antibodies are high.
  • Depression: she feels flat but has no anhedonia, and the bloods explain the fatigue.
  • Addison disease (must not miss): she has type 1 diabetes, but has weight gain, no pigmentation, no postural drop and normal Na and K.

1. Levothyroxine for life: she is young with no heart disease, so give about 1.6 micrograms/kg (ideal body weight) daily, about 100 micrograms. Take it on an empty stomach, 30 to 60 minutes before breakfast and 4 hours apart from iron or calcium. Keep the same brand.
  2. TSH at 6 to 8 weeks and after each dose change; titrate into range, then check yearly. Avoid over-replacement.
  3. Anaemia: B12, folate, IF antibodies, reticulocytes, review the pending blood film (hypersegmented neutrophils, oval macrocytes), iron studies, LFTs and GGT. Never give folate alone.
  4. Coeliac serology (tTG-IgA and total IgA). Check a morning cortisol first if adrenal insufficiency is suspected.
  5. Diabetes: more frequent glucose checks.
  6. Alcohol: no more than 10 standard drinks a week and no more than 4 on any day (NHMRC). Pregnancy: tell us early, because the dose rises.

• Explanation: the immune system has made the thyroid underactive. It is more common with type 1 diabetes, the tablet is daily and for life, and energy returns over weeks to months.
  • Pregnancy: yes, you can; tell us before trying or as soon as you are pregnant, because the dose goes up straight away and TSH is checked early.
  • Palpitations, tremor, feeling hot or weight loss: see the GP; chest pain, a racing irregular heartbeat or collapse: 000.
  • 000 or ED for drowsiness, confusion or feeling very cold and slowed.
  • GP within days for breathlessness, numbness, pins and needles or unsteadiness.
  • Urgent review for a fast-growing neck lump or trouble swallowing or breathing.
  • Follow-up: results in a week, TSH at 6 to 8 weeks.

ddx.dx: Hashimoto (autoimmune) thyroiditis with overt primary hypothyroidism
ddx.for: Three months of fatigue with weight gain, cold intolerance, constipation, dry skin, hair loss and irregular periods; HR 56, a diffuse firm goitre and slow-relaxing reflexes; TSH 52, free T4 4.3 and positive anti-TPO and anti-Tg in a woman with type 1 diabetes.

ddx.dx: Vitamin B12 deficiency from pernicious anaemia
ddx.for: MCV 118 is higher than hypothyroidism usually causes, and she has two autoimmune diseases.
ddx.against: Her neurological examination and tongue are normal, and B12 has not yet been measured.

ddx.for: She drinks about 20 standard drinks a week and eats takeaway twice a week.
ddx.against: Alcohol alone rarely pushes the MCV as high as 118.

ddx.dx: Subacute (de Quervain) thyroiditis in its hypothyroid phase
ddx.against: Her goitre is non-tender, she has had no neck pain, viral illness or thyrotoxic phase, her CRP is normal, and her thyroid antibodies are strongly positive.

ddx.for: She feels flat, wakes unrefreshed and has lost her partner.
ddx.against: She still enjoys her daughter and garden, has no suicidal thoughts, and the bloods explain her fatigue.

ddx.dx: Primary adrenal insufficiency (Addison disease) as part of autoimmune polyglandular syndrome
ddx.for: She has type 1 diabetes and now autoimmune thyroid disease, with fatigue and weakness.
ddx.against: She has gained weight, has no hypos, pigmentation, salt craving or postural drop, and her sodium and potassium are normal.

guide:
In Part 1 the examiner gives findings from the Exam findings only when the candidate says what they examine. Jenny gives each symptom only when asked about it, so the hypothyroid features and the wine are earned by direct questions. The source case gives a large share of its marks to a screen for other causes of fatigue. Credit the cluster item when the candidate covers at least four of its five screening areas.

In Part 2, hand over all three results together and ask the four questions in order. Questions 1 to 3 are a discussion with the supervising GP. For Question 4 Jenny is back in the room, and the person playing her puts her questions while the candidate explains.

Accept a full replacement levothyroxine dose or a lower starting dose with titration. Doses and brands do not need to be exact.

A high-performing candidate characterises the fatigue and asks specifically about hypothyroid symptoms. They screen widely for other causes, including mood and adrenal insufficiency, and quantify the alcohol. They examine the thyroid properly and test the reflexes. In Part 2 they call the result overt primary Hashimoto hypothyroidism and see that an MCV of 118 needs a B12 and folate work-up given her autoimmunity. They start levothyroxine with clear instructions and TSH monitoring, and give specific red flags.

A borderline candidate takes a generic fatigue history and misses the alcohol or the mood screen. They palpate the neck without a swallow, attribute the anaemia to the thyroid alone, or start folate without checking B12. They leave out how to take levothyroxine or when to recheck TSH, or give vague safety netting such as "come back if worse".
explain:
Approach to fatigue

Fatigue is common and non-specific, so the history has to be broad but organised. Characterise it: onset, course, whether it is weakness or sleepiness, severity, modifying factors and impact. Then screen by system:

  • Endocrine: hypo- and hyperthyroidism, diabetes control, adrenal insufficiency.
  • Haematological: anaemia (diet, menstrual and GI blood loss).
  • Malignancy and infection (including TB).
  • Cardiorespiratory: heart failure, COPD, obstructive sleep apnoea.
  • Psychiatric: depression, including anhedonia and suicidal thoughts.
  • Medicines, alcohol and other drugs.

Jenny's history has a clear cluster: weight gain, cold intolerance, constipation, dry skin, hair loss, irregular periods and low mood. Together these point to hypothyroidism.

Hypothyroidism: patterns and causes

  • Primary: TSH high, free T4 low.
  • Secondary (central): TSH low or inappropriately normal with a low free T4. A very low free T4 with only a mildly raised TSH should also raise this possibility.
  • Subclinical: TSH high with a normal free T4.

Low thyroid hormone slows the metabolic rate, causing apathy, slowed thinking, dry skin, hair loss, weight gain and a raised LDL. Slowed gut motility causes constipation, and reduced adrenergic responsiveness and direct cardiac effects cause bradycardia. It also causes a myopathy, slow-relaxing reflexes and, when severe, myxoedema.

Hashimoto thyroiditis is the commonest cause where iodine intake is sufficient (iodine deficiency is the commonest cause worldwide). It is associated with other autoimmune disease, including type 1 diabetes, pernicious anaemia, coeliac disease and Addison disease. Other causes are:

  • postpartum and subacute (de Quervain) thyroiditis;
  • iatrogenic causes: thyroid surgery, radioiodine, amiodarone and lithium;
  • pituitary or hypothalamic disease.

Interpreting Jenny's results

  • Thyroid function and antibodies: TSH 52 with free T4 4.3 is overt primary hypothyroidism. Positive anti-TPO and anti-thyroglobulin antibodies with a diffuse, firm, rubbery, non-tender goitre make this Hashimoto thyroiditis. Without a nodule, no ultrasound is needed. Ultrasound, scintigraphy and biopsy are for a nodular gland.
  • Full blood count: a macrocytic anaemia. The causes of macrocytosis are alcohol and liver disease, B12 or folate deficiency, cytotoxic drugs such as methotrexate, myelodysplasia and hypothyroidism. Hypothyroidism usually causes only a mild macrocytosis, so an MCV of 118 calls for B12 and folate studies. Pernicious anaemia is likely given her autoimmunity, and her drinking may contribute. Never treat with folate alone before B12 deficiency is excluded or treated.
  • Inflammatory markers: the ESR is mildly raised, in keeping with the anaemia (and raised immunoglobulins in autoimmune disease). The CRP is normal, as expected in Hashimoto thyroiditis, and argues against subacute thyroiditis.
  • Electrolytes: normal sodium and potassium make adrenal insufficiency less likely but do not exclude it; early Addison disease often has normal electrolytes, so keep it in mind given her type 1 diabetes and autoimmune thyroid disease.

Further investigations

The source case lists the work-up for fatigue with a suspected thyroid cause: FBE, ESR and CRP, UEC and LFTs, lipids, CK, iron studies, B12 and folate, TFTs (TSH, free T4, free T3), thyroid antibodies (anti-TPO, anti-thyroglobulin, TRAb), and coeliac serology because of her type 1 diabetes. Ultrasound, scintigraphy and biopsy are added if there is a nodule.

Management (eTG)

  • Levothyroxine for life. A young adult without heart disease can start a full replacement dose of about 1.6 micrograms/kg (ideal body weight) daily, about 100 micrograms for Jenny. Older people and those with ischaemic heart disease start low and increase slowly.
  • How to take it: on an empty stomach, separated from iron and calcium, which reduce absorption.
  • Monitoring: check TSH 6 to 8 weeks after starting or changing the dose and titrate to a TSH in the reference range, then check yearly once stable.
  • Over-replacement causes palpitations, arrhythmia (especially AF), angina, tremor and osteoporosis.
  • Adrenal insufficiency: if it is suspected, treat it before starting thyroxine, which can otherwise precipitate an adrenal crisis.
  • Diabetes: monitor glucose more closely as she becomes euthyroid, because her insulin needs may change.
  • B12: check it, and replace it if low.
  • Alcohol: reduce to no more than 10 standard drinks a week and no more than 4 on any day (NHMRC).
  • Pregnancy: levothyroxine requirements rise in pregnancy, so she should plan pregnancy with her GP, aim for a TSH below 2.5 mIU/L before conception, and have the dose increased and TSH checked as soon as pregnancy is confirmed.

Complications to know

  • Myxoedema coma: managed in ICU with IV hydrocortisone, cautious IV thyroxine and passive rewarming.
  • Hashimoto encephalopathy.
  • Vascular disease from dyslipidaemia.
  • Carpal tunnel syndrome.
  • Thyroid lymphoma: rare, and presents as a rapidly enlarging goitre.

Safety netting

  • Too much thyroxine: palpitations, tremor, heat intolerance, weight loss or insomnia need GP review. Chest pain or collapse needs 000.
  • Severe hypothyroidism: increasing drowsiness, confusion or feeling very cold needs ED.
  • Anaemia or B12 deficiency: breathlessness, numbness, pins and needles or unsteadiness need prompt review.
  • The neck: a rapidly growing neck lump or trouble swallowing or breathing needs urgent assessment.
  • Mood: worsening mood or thoughts of self-harm need same-day help.
points: Screen fatigue by system (endocrine, haematological, malignancy and infection, cardiorespiratory and sleep, psychiatric, alcohol and medicines), then look for a cluster such as weight gain, cold intolerance, constipation, dry skin and hair loss.
High TSH with low free T4 is primary hypothyroidism; low or inappropriately normal TSH with low free T4 suggests a central cause; high TSH with normal free T4 is subclinical.

Hashimoto thyroiditis is the commonest cause where iodine is sufficient and clusters with type 1 diabetes, pernicious anaemia, coeliac disease and Addison disease. Screen for them, and treat adrenal insufficiency before starting thyroxine.

Hypothyroidism causes at most a mild macrocytosis. Any unexplained macrocytosis needs B12 and folate studies. An MCV above 110 makes hypothyroidism or alcohol alone an unlikely explanation, and folate must never be given alone before B12 deficiency is excluded or treated.

Levothyroxine is lifelong. Take it on an empty stomach, apart from iron and calcium. Check TSH 6 to 8 weeks after each change, avoid over-replacement (AF, angina, osteoporosis), and increase the dose early in pregnancy.
